title: Suffering calmly
hook: a carpenter's bubble, and a hymn about one who sees gold and clay the same

segments.voice: Yesterday, freedom of conscience: the ninth Guru went to Delhi for people whose thread he didn't wear. Your line was their faith, their right.

A carpenter's level is a simple tool: a little tube of liquid with one bubble trapped inside. Tilt the board one way and the bubble runs off. Tilt it the other way and it runs off again. Only when the board is true does the bubble sit still, right between the two lines. Plenty of days feel like a board tipped back and forth. Good news, and the bubble runs. Bad news, and it runs the other way. Guru Tegh Bahadur wrote a hymn about a person whose bubble stays in the middle.
screen: `A TUBE, ONE BUBBLE.` → `TILT, AND IT RUNS.` → `A PERSON WHO STAYS LEVEL.`

segments.voice: The hymn is in Raga Sorath, paraphrased. The one who, in pain, does not take pain as pain. Who has no clinging to pleasure, and no fear. Who looks on gold as clay. Who is moved neither by slander nor by praise, and is free of greed, attachment and pride. Who stays the same in joy and sorrow, in honor and dishonor. In that one, the hymn says, the Lord lives; such a person blends with the Lord like water into water. Notice what the hymn doesn't say. It doesn't say the level person feels nothing, or that pain isn't real. It keeps returning to pairs: pain and pleasure, praise and slander, gold and clay. The point isn't escaping one side. It's not being thrown by either. A raise and a rejection both meet the same steady person. And this wasn't theory for the man who wrote it. His life ended in Delhi, and Sikh tradition remembers him meeting it calmly. A short salok of his says the same in fewer words: the one untouched by pleasure and pain, by greed, attachment and pride, is the very image of the Lord. A normal day asks nothing like that, but the bubble still runs: a text that stings, a compliment that goes to your head. Notice the tilt, and let the bubble come back. And if pain right now is more than you can carry, staying level never means staying alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `IN PAIN, NOT TAKING PAIN AS PAIN.` · `GOLD AND CLAY, PRAISE AND SLANDER.` · `WATER BLENDING INTO WATER.` · `NOT THROWN BY EITHER SIDE.` · then, large: `LEVEL.`

segments.voice: Notice the mood you're in right now and name it plainly, tired, happy, worried, flat, without pushing it away or feeding it. Picture the bubble in the level, and with each breath out let it settle a little nearer the middle, noticing whatever pulls it up or down. If you pray, rest in Waheguru on each breath.
Suffering calmly. The ninth Guru's hymn praises one who meets pain and pleasure, praise and slander, gold and clay the same, and stays level. Today's word.
Your line: level. Not numb, just not thrown, whichever way the board tips. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns, such as this one in Raga Sorath, in kirtan, and his saloks on meeting pleasure and pain alike are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

chat.says: That hymn about pain not being pain: is it telling people to feel nothing?
options: No. Pain is real; the hymn is about staying level, not thrown by either side.
Yes. The aim is to go numb so pain and joy stop reaching you.
No. It's saying only pleasure is real, so chase it and ignore the rest.
chat.meaning: The Sorath hymn doesn't ask for numbness. It keeps naming pairs, pain and pleasure, praise and slander, and praises the one who stays level.

Raga Sorath.meaning: a musical mode of the Guru Granth Sahib
